mustMemorise: $\sum x = n\bar{x}$ recovers a group's total from its mean

Counts and totals add when groups are pooled; means, variances and standard deviations do not
Never average two means unless the groups are the same size, and never average two standard deviations
Taking a group out subtracts its count as well as its two totals

Machine A packed 12 boxes of bulbs with a mean of 25 bulbs and a standard deviation of 4 bulbs.
Machine B packed 8 boxes with a mean of 35 bulbs and a standard deviation of 6 bulbs.
Calculate the mean and the standard deviation of the number of bulbs per box over all 20 boxes.

steps.working: Machine A: $\sum x = 12 \times 25 = 300$. Machine B: $\sum x = 8 \times 35 = 280$.
steps.decision: Turn each mean back into a total, because totals are the only things that add across groups. A mean is a total that has already been shared out, and you cannot share out twice.
The combined mean sits nearer 25 than 35, because machine A filled more boxes. Averaging the two means would have given 30, which is what the reports keep seeing.

options: 29, because machine A's 12 boxes outnumber machine B's 8
30, because it is halfway between the two means
35, because machine B has the higher mean
whyMenu.explain: The combined mean is a weighted average. Halfway would only be right if both machines had filled the same number of boxes.

steps.working: $\sum x^{2} = n\left(\sigma^{2} + \bar{x}^{2}\right)$, so machine A gives $12\left(4^{2} + 25^{2}\right) = 7692$ and machine B gives $8\left(6^{2} + 35^{2}\right) = 10088$.
steps.decision: Rearranging the sheet's formula gives the sum of squares back from a standard deviation. Both terms are needed: drop the $\sigma^{2}$ and the spread inside each machine disappears.
Add the two sums of squares. This is the step the reports describe candidates skipping: they add the raw values, or square the total, instead of adding two sums of squares.

Back into the sheet's formula with the combined totals and the combined mean. Notice the answer is larger than either machine's own standard deviation, because the gap between the two means is itself spread.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: A mean of $29$ bulbs per box and a standard deviation of $6.93$ bulbs

items.stem: Before the lesson, a check on something you already know. Eight boxes hold a mean of 64 items each. What is the total number of items?
items.skill: Turning a mean back into a total (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.feedback: Yes: $8 \times 64 = 512$. This one line starts every question in this topic.
That is the mean again. The total is the mean multiplied by how many boxes there are.
That divides where it should multiply. The mean is already the total shared out, so multiplying puts it back together.

items.stem: Before the lesson: five values have $\sum x = 120$. What is their mean?
items.skill: Mean from a total (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.feedback: That is the total. Sharing it over the five values gives the mean.
That multiplies where it should divide. The total is already the sum of all five.

items.stem: Before the lesson, and you are not meant to know this yet: two classes sit the same test and you know each class's mean. What would you need before you could find the mean of both classes together?
items.skill: Why a mean alone is not enough (new here, so a guess is fine)

options.text: How many pupils are in each class
options.feedback: Exactly. Without the two class sizes the means cannot be weighted, and averaging them would be a guess.

options.text: Nothing more: average the two means
options.feedback: That is right only when the classes are the same size. It is the most reported error on this question.
Those do not enter the mean at all. What is missing is how many pupils each mean is spread over.

items.stem: Before the lesson, and this one is new: $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum x^{2}}{n} - \bar{x}^{2}}$. Rearranged for $\sum x^{2}$, what do you get?

options.feedback: Yes. Square both sides, add $\bar{x}^{2}$, multiply by $n$. That is the key that unlocks every pooled question.
The square belongs on each term separately, not on the bracket. Squaring the sum introduces a cross term that is not there.
That drops the $\sigma^{2}$, which is the only part carrying the spread. It is the most common slip in the recovery step.

items.stem: Machine A filled 12 boxes with a mean of 25; machine B filled 8 boxes with a mean of 35. What is the combined mean?
items.skill: Weighting each mean by its own n

options.feedback: Yes: $\dfrac{300 + 280}{20} = 29$. It leans towards machine A, which filled more boxes.
That is halfway between the two means, which would need 12 boxes and 8 boxes to be equal. They are not.
That is machine B's own mean. The combined mean has to sit between the two.

items.stem: A group has $n = 12$, $\bar{x} = 25$ and $\sigma = 4$. What is $\sum x^{2}$?

options.feedback: That is $n\bar{x}^{2}$ with $\sigma^{2}$ dropped. The 4 is the only thing in the question carrying the spread.
That is the square of the total. A sum of squares is always much smaller than the square of the sum.

items.stem: Two groups are pooled. Which pair of quantities can simply be added?
items.skill: Knowing what adds and what does not

options.feedback: Yes. Those are running totals over the values, so putting the groups together just adds them.

options.text: The two means and the two standard deviations
options.feedback: Neither adds. Both are totals that have already been divided, and dividing cannot be undone by adding.
Variances do not add either, because the gap between the two group means adds spread of its own.

items.stem: Machine A has $\sigma = 4$ and machine B has $\sigma = 6$. The combined standard deviation is 6.93. Why is it bigger than both?

options.text: The gap between the two group means is extra spread in the pooled set
options.feedback: Yes. Even if each machine were perfectly consistent, boxes from the two machines would still differ.

options.text: Because standard deviations always grow when you add data
options.feedback: Not always. Pooling two groups with the same mean can leave the spread almost unchanged.

options.text: Because the larger group has more influence
options.feedback: Size decides the weighting, not the widening. What widens the spread is the distance between the means.

items.stem: All 15 walkers have $\sum x^{2} = 5235$ and 5 of them have $\sum x^{2} = 1953$. What is $\sum x^{2}$ for the rest, and how many are there?

options.feedback: Yes. Subtract the sums of squares and subtract the counts: 15 minus 5 is 10.
The total is right but the count is not. Once the family is out there are only 10 walkers left to divide by.
The family's distances were subtracted without being squared. Take 1953 off, not 95.

items.stem: A pooled calculation reaches $\dfrac{\sum x^{2}}{n} = 889$ with $\bar{x} = 29$. What is the standard deviation?
items.skill: Subtracting the mean squared, then rooting

options.feedback: Yes: $889 - 841 = 48$, and its root is 6.93.
That is the variance, the number under the root. One step is missing.
The mean squared was never subtracted, so that is about the size of a box count rather than its spread.

items.stem: The 8 players on team A average 64 and all 20 players average 70. What is team B's mean?
items.skill: Finding a missing group's mean from the totals

options.feedback: Yes: $1400 - 512 = 888$ over 12 players.
That adds the gap to the overall mean once, as if the teams were the same size. Team A has 8 players and team B 12.
That is team A's mean, which the question gave you. Check which group the answer line names.

items.stem: You have both groups' totals and you are about to find the pooled standard deviation. Which mean goes into the formula?
items.skill: Using the combined mean, not a group mean

options.text: The combined mean of all the values
options.feedback: Yes. The formula measures spread about the mean of the set you are describing, which is now the pooled set.

options.text: The mean of the larger group
options.feedback: That would measure spread about the wrong centre and give an answer that is too large.

options.text: The average of the two group means
options.feedback: That is not the pooled mean unless the groups are the same size, and it is the error the reports name most often.

parts.stem:
Calculate the standard deviation of the number of bulbs per box over all 20 boxes.
You must show your working.

scheme.for: $\sum x^{2} = n\left(\sigma^{2} + \bar{x}^{2}\right)$ used for at least one group

hints: Then use the combined mean 29 in the sheet's formula.
parts.workedSolution:
Machine A: $\sum x^{2} = 12\left(4^{2} + 25^{2}\right) = 7692$.
Machine B: $\sum x^{2} = 8\left(6^{2} + 35^{2}\right) = 10088$.
Together $\sum x^{2} = 17780$ and $\bar{x} = 29$.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{17780}{20} - 29^{2}} = \sqrt{48} = 6.93$ bulbs.

commonErrors.feedback: The two standard deviations have been averaged. Spread does not combine that way: the two groups sit at different means, and that gap adds spread of its own. Work through $\sum x^{2}$ and the answer is 6.93.
Each group's $\sum x^{2}$ was taken as $n\bar{x}^{2}$, with the $\sigma^{2}$ term dropped. Nothing then carries the spread inside the groups, so the answer comes out far too small.
$\left(\sum x\right)^{2}$ has gone into the formula in place of $\sum x^{2}$. Recover each group's sum of squares from its own standard deviation; together they come to 17780.
That is the combined variance. The three method marks are safe; the last working mark is the square root, $\sqrt{48} = 6.93$.

context.setting: Times on a climbing route: five beginners listed, the club summarised

parts.stem:
Five beginners took 21, 27, 24, 30, 18 minutes on a climbing route, and the 15 club members behind them had a mean of 30 minutes with a standard deviation of 4 minutes.
Calculate the standard deviation of the times of all 20 climbers.
You must show your working.
hints: Square the five listed times and add: 2970.
parts.workedSolution:
Beginners: $\sum x = 120$ and $\sum x^{2} = 2970$.
Club: $\sum x = 450$ and $\sum x^{2} = 15\left(4^{2} + 30^{2}\right) = 13740$.
Together $\sum x = 570$, $\sum x^{2} = 16710$ and $\bar{x} = 28.5$.

context.setting: A garden centre packing boxes of bulbs on two machines

parts.stem:
A garden centre packs boxes of daffodil bulbs on two machines.
On one morning, machine A packed 12 boxes with a mean of 25 bulbs per box and a standard deviation of 4 bulbs.
Machine B packed 8 boxes with a mean of 35 bulbs per box and a standard deviation of 6 bulbs.
Calculate the mean number of bulbs per box for all 20 boxes.
hints: Do not average the two means.
Each machine's total is its own mean times its own number of boxes.
parts.workedSolution:
Machine A total $= 300$; machine B total $= 280$.
$\bar{x} = \dfrac{580}{20} = 29$ bulbs per box.

commonErrors.feedback: The two means have been averaged, which the examiners see every year on this question. It is only correct when the groups are the same size. Weighted by 12 and 8 boxes, the mean is 29.

parts.stem:
Calculate the standard deviation of the number of bulbs per box for all 20 boxes.
You must show your working.

scheme.for: $\sum x^{2} = n\left(\sigma^{2} + \bar{x}^{2}\right)$ applied to machine A or machine B

hints: Each machine's $\sum x^{2}$ comes from its own mean and standard deviation.
Use the combined mean 29 from part (a).
parts.workedSolution:
Machine A: $\sum x^{2} = 12\left(4^{2} + 25^{2}\right) = 7692$.
Machine B: $\sum x^{2} = 8\left(6^{2} + 35^{2}\right) = 10088$.
$\sum x^{2} = 17780$, and the combined mean is 29.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{17780}{20} - 29^{2}} = \sqrt{889 - 841} = \sqrt{48} = 6.93$ bulbs.

commonErrors.feedback: Averaging the two standard deviations gives that. Spread has to be rebuilt from $\sum x^{2}$, because the gap between the two machine means adds spread of its own; the answer is 6.93.
$\left(\sum x\right)^{2}$ has been used where $\sum x^{2}$ belongs. The sum of squares is recovered group by group from each standard deviation and comes to 17780.
Each $\sum x^{2}$ was built as $n\bar{x}^{2}$ with the $\sigma^{2}$ term dropped, so the answer measures only the gap between the machines and none of the spread inside them.
That is the variance. Three marks are safe; the fourth is the square root, $\sqrt{48} = 6.93$.

parts.stem:
Over 25 hours a bakery baked a mean of 54 loaves an hour. The 10 hours of the early shift had a mean of 48 loaves an hour.
Calculate the mean number of loaves an hour on the 15 hours of the late shift.
hints: The late shift ran for 15 hours.
parts.workedSolution:
All 25 hours: $\sum x = 1350$.
Early shift: $\sum x = 480$.
Late shift: $\sum x = 870$ over 15 hours, so the mean is 58 loaves an hour.

commonErrors.feedback: The overall mean and the early shift's mean have been averaged. Totals are the only things that subtract cleanly: 1350 minus 480 over 15 hours gives 58.
That is the early shift's mean, which the question already gave you. The answer line wants the late shift: 58 loaves an hour.

parts.stem:
Over the same 25 hours the standard deviation was 9.09 loaves an hour, and on the early shift it was 5.
Calculate the standard deviation of the number of loaves an hour on the late shift.

scheme.for: $\sum x^{2}$ for all 25 hours from 9.09 and 54

hints: Rebuild $\sum x^{2}$ for all 25 hours, then for the early shift.
Divide the late shift's sum of squares by 15, not by 25.

commonErrors.feedback: The overall and early-shift standard deviations have been averaged. Only $\sum x$ and $\sum x^{2}$ subtract; rebuild both and the late shift's figure is 9.
That is the late shift's variance. The answer line wants its square root, 9 loaves an hour.

The two variances have been subtracted and rooted, as if spread could be taken apart without the means. The gap between the shift means is part of the overall spread, so that route always comes out short; the answer is 9.

findTheMistake.stem: Órlaith was asked for the mean number of bulbs per box over all 20 boxes, given machine A (12 boxes, mean 25) and machine B (8 boxes, mean 35). Her working:
studentWorking: machine A mean 25, machine B mean 35
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 averages the two means. That is only the combined mean when the groups are the same size, and here machine A filled 12 boxes against machine B's 8.
correction: combined mean = 580 over 20 = 29 bulbs per box
findTheMistake.feedback: No method mark is available here, because the route cannot reach the answer: an unweighted average throws away the box counts, which are the whole point of the question. Turn each mean into a total first, add the totals, then divide by 20. The answer is 29 bulbs per box, and it leans towards machine A because machine A filled more boxes.

findTheMistake.stem: Conor was asked for the standard deviation of all 20 climbers' times, given the five beginners' times 21, 27, 24, 30, 18 and the club's 15 times (mean 30, standard deviation 4). His working:
studentWorking: club sum of x squared = 15(4 squared + 30 squared) = 13740
beginners sum of x = 120, so their sum of x squared = 120 squared = 14400
sd = square root of (28140 over 20 minus 28.5 squared) = 24.39
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 squares the beginners' total. Their sum of squares is 21^{2} + 27^{2} + 24^{2} + 30^{2} + 18^{2} = 2970, which is a different and much smaller number than 14400.
correction: sd = square root of (16710 over 20 minus 28.5 squared) = 4.82
findTheMistake.feedback: The recovery of the club's sum of squares is right, so the method mark for $\sum x^{2} = n\left(\sigma^{2} + \bar{x}^{2}\right)$ is safe. The working mark is lost at line 2: a sum of squares squares each value on its own. Examiners report candidates adding a group's values unsquared or squaring their total, and both routes end in an answer far too large. With 2970 in place, the standard deviation is 4.82 minutes.

findTheMistake.stem: Méabh was asked for the standard deviation of the other 10 walkers' distances. Her working:
studentWorking: all 15: sum of x = 270, sum of x squared = 5235
family: sum of x = 95, sum of x squared = 1953
others: sum of x = 175, sum of x squared = 3282, mean = 17.5
sd = square root of (3282 minus 17.5 squared) = 54.55
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 4 never divides the sum of squares by the number of walkers. The formula is $\dfrac{\sum x^{2}}{n} - \bar{x}^{2}$, and here $n$ is 10, not 15 and not 1.
correction: others: n = 10, sum of x = 175, sum of x squared = 3282
sd = square root of (3282 over 10 minus 17.5 squared) = square root of 21.95 = 4.69
findTheMistake.feedback: Three marks are already safe: the whole set's totals, the family's totals and the subtraction are all correct, which is further than most candidates get. The final working mark needs the division by 10. Examiners describe exactly this: the right sum of squares reached, and then the division forgotten. Divide first, subtract the mean squared, then root, and the answer is 4.69 km.

prompts.prompt: How do you get $\sum x$ back from $n$ and the mean?
How do you get $\sum x^{2}$ back from $n$, the mean and the standard deviation?
prompts.answer: $\sum x^{2} = n\left(\sigma^{2} + \bar{x}^{2}\right)$, from rearranging the sheet's formula.

prompts.prompt: The five steps for the standard deviation of two pooled groups.
prompts.answer: 1 Recover $\sum x$ for each group. 2 Recover $\sum x^{2}$ for each group. 3 Add both totals and add the counts. 4 Divide for the combined mean. 5 Put the combined totals into the sheet's formula and take the root.

prompts.prompt: When is the average of two group means the same as their combined mean?
prompts.answer: Only when the two groups are the same size. Otherwise each mean has to be weighted by its own $n$.

prompts.prompt: Which quantities add when two groups are pooled, and which do not?
prompts.answer: $\sum x$, $\sum x^{2}$ and $n$ add. Means, variances and standard deviations do not.

prompts.prompt: Why is a pooled standard deviation usually larger than either group's own?
prompts.answer: The distance between the two group means is extra spread in the pooled set, on top of the spread inside each group.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the statistics of the group that is left when a listed sub-group is taken out?
prompts.answer: Rebuild $\sum x$ and $\sum x^{2}$ for the whole set, subtract the sub-group's $\sum x$ and $\sum x^{2}$, subtract the counts, then use the sheet's formula with the new $n$.

prompts.prompt: You have found $\sum x^{2}$ for the remaining group. What is the step candidates most often forget next?
prompts.answer: Dividing by the remaining group's own $n$ before subtracting the square of its mean.

prompts.prompt: A group of 8 has mean 64 and the whole squad of 20 has mean 70. How do you find the other 12 players' mean?
prompts.answer: Totals: $20 \times 70 = 1400$ and $8 \times 64 = 512$, so the other twelve total $888$ and their mean is $74$.

prompts.prompt: What does a negative value under the square root tell you in a pooled calculation?
prompts.answer: That something has been subtracted the wrong way round, usually $\sum x^{2}$ and $\bar{x}^{2}$ swapped, or the sum of squares divided by the wrong $n$. A variance is never negative.

findings.asked: Mean and standard deviation of 14 results from two groups' data.
findings.wentWrong: Many averaged the girls' mean and the boys' mean (83.75); for the SD, the girls' sum of squares was found but the boys' values were added unsquared, or the square of their sum was used.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Recovered sum of x and sum of x squared for each group from n, mean and SD, added them, and recomputed.
findings.rule: Combine totals (sum x, sum x squared), never averages.

findings.asked: Mean of 14 tests from the means of two subsets; SD of all 14.
findings.wentWrong: A few added 69 and 83 and halved; about half managed the SD - it was done well or not at all.
findings.rule: n1 mean1 + n2 mean2 over n1 + n2.

findings.asked: Mean speed of cars from combined groups; SD.
findings.wentWrong: Some found the lorries' mean instead; for the SD some got the total sum of squares (14560) but could not extract the cars' sum of squares (10187) or forgot to divide by 10.
findings.rule: Sum of x squared = n(SD squared + mean squared) for each group.

findings.asked: Adjust a mean and SD when values are corrected.
findings.wentWrong: 108.4 x 14 instead of x 15; adjusted using only one of the two values; in the SD part the sum of squares was adjusted by adding the raw difference (182) rather than the squares; some squared sum x instead of summing x squared.
findings.rule: Remove the old value and its square, add the new value and its square, then recompute with the correct n.

insight.ruleToRemember: Work with totals: sum x = n x mean and sum x squared = n(SD squared + mean squared); add, remove or replace the actual values and their squares; recompute mean and SD from the new totals with the new n.
insight.aStarSignal: Correcting a data set (wrong value replaced) and recomputing the SD via the sums of squares.
